opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question, and I think the honest answer is that we don't really know yet, and anyone who gives you a precise number is probably guessing.

But let me frame it this way. A lot of people in our field have this mental model where intelligence is mostly a function of scale: more GPUs, more data, more parameters, and eventually you get something that can answer the deep questions. And scaling has absolutely worked, I'm not denying that. But I've always been a little skeptical that compute alone is the bottleneck for the kinds of questions you're describing, questions about life, about the physical universe, about how things actually work.

If you think about how humans came to understand the universe, it wasn't by reading more text. It was by observing, building instruments, running experiments, forming abstractions about the world. A child learns intuitive physics long before learning language. So my view is that a lot of the remaining progress depends on systems that can perceive and model the world, visually, spatially, causally, not just predict the next token. That's partly why I care so much about vision and world models.

Now, does that need a lot of compute? Probably yes, maybe even more than language, because the visual world is so much richer and higher-dimensional than text. But I think the question isn't just "how much compute," it's "compute spent on what." If we pour enormous resources into the wrong objective, we just get a very expensive system that's very good at imitating the internet.

There's also something humbling here. The human brain runs on roughly twenty watts. Evolution found a remarkably efficient solution. So I suspect there are big algorithmic and representational breakthroughs still waiting, and those could change the compute equation by orders of magnitude.

So my short answer: compute is necessary, but it's not sufficient. The more interesting challenge for researchers, especially in academia where we don't have the biggest clusters, is figuring out the right ideas, so that when the compute is there, we're using it to actually understand the world rather than just memorize it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute needs and world models, but never suggests using the entire universe as a computer.

r002.rationale: The response gives no suggestion that the ultimate answer might be forty-two.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question, and I think it's a healthy one to ask, because the honest answer is that we don't actually know how much compute it takes to answer those questions, and I'm not sure "more compute" is even the right axis.

Let me give you my perspective as someone who has spent most of my career working on vision. When people talk about scaling, they usually mean scaling language models: more parameters, more tokens, more GPUs. And that has clearly worked for a certain class of problems, problems where the knowledge is already written down by humans. But questions about life and the universe are mostly not like that. The universe doesn't come with a text corpus. It comes with observations: images, videos, measurements, signals. Most of the information in the physical world has never been described in language, and arguably can't be fully described in language.

So I actually think the bottleneck is not raw compute, it's the learning paradigm. If you want a system to understand physics, or biology, or how a cell behaves, you need it to learn from the world the way a scientist does, from perception and interaction, not just from reading papers about the world. And right now we don't have a learning recipe for that which is as efficient as what we have for text. Self-supervised learning on visual data is still, in my view, an unsolved problem in a deep sense. We can train big models, but the representations they learn are not as structured or as grounded as we'd like.

The second thing I'd say is that we should be a bit careful about the framing that compute is the scarce resource. Humans are the existence proof. A child learns an incredible amount about the physical world with something like a few years of visual experience and roughly 20 watts of power. The brain is not doing trillions of gradient steps on an internet-scale dataset. So there's clearly a huge gap in sample efficiency and energy efficiency between what we do and what nature does. That gap tells me the answer isn't simply to keep multiplying the number of GPUs. We're missing something architecturally and algorithmically, and I'd rather spend my time on that than on just making the same thing bigger.

That said, I'm not anti-scaling. I think the right mental model is that compute is the amplifier, and the ideas are the signal. If your ideas are wrong, scaling just makes them wrong faster and at greater cost. If your ideas are right, scaling is what lets them become transformative. So for questions as hard as how life works or how the universe works, I'd expect we'll need both: fundamentally better ways of learning from raw, unlabeled observation, and then very large compute to apply them at the scale of real scientific data, telescopes, microscopes, simulations.

And honestly, I think the exciting part is that this is still open. In some areas of AI the field has converged and the work is mostly engineering. But learning from the physical world is still a place where a good idea from a small group can change the picture. For me that's much more interesting than asking how many chips we need.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute as an amplifier and the need for large-scale compute, but does not suggest using the entire universe as a computer.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that the answer might be forty-two.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by answering those questions. You can imagine having an enormous amount of computation, but if you haven’t formulated the right question, it may not get you very far. In that sense, the bottleneck is not just compute—it’s also our understanding of what to compute.

For questions about life and the universe, we need observations, experiments, and models that we can test. More computational resources can help us simulate things and discover patterns, but that doesn’t automatically translate into understanding. The exciting possibility is that AI could help us formulate better hypotheses, so computation becomes part of the process of asking better questions, too.

r001.rationale: The response discusses enormous computation, simulations, and models, but does not suggest using the entire universe as a computer.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention forty-two as a possible ultimate answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by answering those questions. You can imagine needing enormous computational resources to simulate the universe, but having more compute doesn’t automatically mean you understand it. You still need to know what question to ask, what to model, and what evidence would count as an answer.

For me, the exciting possibility is that computation can help us discover patterns we couldn’t see before. But I wouldn’t assume that every deep question about life is simply waiting for a bigger computer. Some of the difficulty is computational, and some of it is conceptual.

r001.rationale: The response mentions enormous compute and simulating the universe, but does not suggest using the entire universe itself as a computer.
